title: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: DEEP OCEAN MISSION
body_text:
The National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES), is entrusted with developing technologies for the reliable and sustainable harvesting of polymetallic nodules from the deep ocean. A seabed mining system has been developed, for which mobility and system-powering trials were successfully undertaken at a depth of 5270 m at the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB) site allocated by the International Seabed Authority (ISA). In addition, NIOT has undertaken the development of nodule collection and crushing components in accordance with ISA guidelines.
Ministry of Earth Sciences has signed contracts with the International Seabed Authority (ISA) for exploration of seabed minerals, namely Polymetallic Nodules (PMN) and Polymetallic Sulphides (PMS) in the Indian Ocean in the areas beyond National jurisdiction. The Resource Assessment and t he Environmental Impact Assessment studies are carried out as per the contractual obligations and guidelines set out by the ISA. Multidisciplinary Oceanographic Studies are conducted in the Indian contract areas under the exploration contract to establish baseline environmental conditions and assess the possible effects of exploration activities on deep sea ecosystems. Presently, only the activities related to exploration of deep seabed minerals in the international seabed are permitted.
This information was given by the Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Earth Sciences Dr. Jitendra Singh in a written reply in Lok Sabha today.
******
NKR/JKP

enrichment.summary: In a Lok Sabha written reply, Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh stated that NIOT, Chennai has developed a deep-sea mining system that successfully underwent mobility and power trials at 5270 m depth in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB), a site allocated by the International Seabed Authority (ISA). The Ministry of Earth Sciences holds ISA exploration contracts for Polymetallic Nodules and Polymetallic Sulphides in international waters of the Indian Ocean, under which resource assessment, environmental impact studies, and baseline oceanographic surveys are being conducted. Currently, only exploration (not commercial mining) of deep seabed minerals is permitted under ISA rules.
enrichment.context:
This update relates to India's Deep Ocean Mission, launched in 2021 by the Ministry of Earth Sciences, aimed at exploring deep-sea resources, biodiversity, and developing technologies for sustainable ocean resource utilization and marine biodiversity conservation. India is one of the few countries to hold 'Pioneer Investor' status with the ISA, having secured exploration rights over a 75,000 sq km area in the Central Indian Ocean Basin for polymetallic nodules since 1987, later expanded with contracts for polymetallic sulphides in the Indian Ocean ridge system near Rodrigues Triple Junction. Polymetallic nodules and sulphides contain strategically important metals like nickel, cobalt, copper, and manganese, critical for batteries, electronics, and clean energy technologies, making seabed mining geopolitically and economically significant amid global supply chain concerns over critical minerals.

The International Seabed Authority, established under UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea), regulates mineral-related activities in the 'Area' — the seabed beyond national jurisdiction, treated as the 'common heritage of mankind'. While exploration is permitted under existing contracts, the ISA has not yet finalized regulations for commercial exploitation (mining), reflecting global debates over environmental risks to fragile deep-sea ecosystems versus the economic imperative for critical mineral security. India's achievement of trials at 5270 m depth places it among a small group of nations demonstrating deep-sea mining-capable technology, relevant to its ambitions of becoming self-reliant in critical minerals and enhancing its blue economy footprint.

prelims_questions.question: The 'Central Indian Ocean Basin', frequently mentioned in the context of India's Deep Ocean Mission, is significant because it is:
options: An area allocated to India by the International Seabed Authority for exploration of polymetallic nodules
A designated Exclusive Economic Zone of India for fishing rights
A UNESCO World Heritage marine site
A naval exercise zone under the Indian Navy
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states that trials were conducted at a CIOB site allocated by the ISA for polymetallic nodule exploration, consistent with India's long-standing pioneer investor status in this basin.

prelims_questions.question: Which of the following statements about the International Seabed Authority (ISA) is correct?
options: It permits full-scale commercial mining of seabed minerals in international waters
It was established under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) to regulate activities in the seabed beyond national jurisdiction
It is a specialized agency of the World Trade Organization
It only regulates seabed resources within countries' territorial waters
prelims_questions.explanation: The ISA, established under UNCLOS, regulates mineral-related activities in the 'Area' beyond national jurisdiction; currently only exploration, not commercial exploitation, is permitted, as noted in the release.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of India's Deep Ocean Mission in the context of critical mineral security and the blue economy. What are the environmental challenges associated with deep seabed mining?

Examine the role of the International Seabed Authority in regulating exploration and exploitation of resources in the international seabed area. How does India's engagement with the ISA reflect its maritime strategic interests?
